narrative:
The model estimated a 67% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it judged failure more likely than passing. Because your law school application was denied on that basis, the decision reflects that this predicted risk was considered too high, not a finding that you cannot succeed.

The strongest influence was your third-year class standing: you were in decile 2, while accepted students averaged around decile 6. This pushed the prediction most strongly toward likely bar failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the next most important factor; it is well below the accepted-student average of about 37 and also pushed toward failure. In contrast, your undergraduate GPA of 3.50 was above the accepted average of about 3.23 and was the main factor pushing toward passing, but it was not enough to outweigh the other two concerns.

To move forward, ask admissions for feedback, strengthen the areas that weighed most heavily, such as retaking the LSAT if feasible, and provide a clear plan showing improved academic and bar-exam readiness. Consider reapplication once you can present stronger evidence that the risk has been addressed.
